newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: Moldova prime minister warns of unrest before vote.
newsitem.headline: Moldova prime minister warns of unrest before vote.

text.p: Moldovan Prime Minister Andrei Sangheli warned on Friday of trouble on the streets before Sunday's presidential election run-off and reaffirmed his government would resign once a new president is elected.

"A number of actions to whip up the situation in the period before the presidential run-off are being prepared," Sangheli, who was eliminated from the presidential race in the first round two weeks ago, said in a radio address.

Sangheli, who has thrown his support behind parliament speaker Petru Lucinschi who is opposing President Mircea Snegur, said he expected huge unauthorised rallies which could destabilise the situation in the capital Chisinau.
The prime minister has already ordered the security forces to tighten control over their armed units.
Bitterness has marked the campaign in a country which has seen civil war and a schism in the military in recent years.
About 300 students chanted anti-government slogans through Chisinau on Wednesday and called for more pro-Snegur marches.
Snegur, who has been president since independence in 1991, and Lucinschi, are running neck and neck.

Snegur won 39 percent in the November 17 first round and has won the backing of a pro-Romanian nationalist who polled nine percent. Lucinschi, who came second with 28 percent, has been endorsed by Sangheli and Moldova's communists.
The two rivals have much in common -- both are 56, come from northern peasant stock and were top communists in Soviet days.
But the race has polarised the tiny state of 4.3 million people sandwiched between Romania and Ukraine.
Snegur, supported by groups seeking closer ties with ethnic and linguistic kin in Romania, wants to plant the country firmly in the Western camp.
He promises quicker market reforms if he secures backing for constitutional change to strengthen the presidency.

Lucinschi, appealing to those who fear submersion in a greater Romania and hanker for the security of Soviet communism, says Chisinau must not turn its back on Moscow, which, among other things, supplies the bulk of its energy.
Openly backed by state television and many newspapers, Lucinschi accuses Snegur of wanting to turn the largely honorific presidency into a "dictatorship".

Anxious not to alienate the 35 percent Russian-speaking minority, Snegur responds that Moldova wants "good relations" with Russia. But he acknowledges he sees the East mainly as a huge market for Moldovan produce.
The tall and bulky Snegur has led an aggressive and populist campaign. He bemoans the "hardships caused by the rule of the corrupt government which must resign."

In an earlier attempt to take on the government, Snegur tried in March to sack the defence minister on corruption charges without Sangheli's consent. The move dangerously split the army, but the Constitutional Court told Snegur to back off.
Lucinschi presents himself as a moderate centre-leftist similiar to many of Eastern Europe's former communists.
The issue of ties to the West or East is painful in Moldova, carved by former Soviet doctator Josef Stalin out of mostly Romanian territory in 1940.

The 700,000 mostly Slavic-speaking people east of the Dnestr river, along the Ukrainian border, broke away in 1990 for fear of being subsumed by Romania. Hundreds died in a 1992 civil war there. It was ended by Russian army intervention.
